author: Unsigned statement (corpus lists General Conference of SDA)
work: Fundamental Principles of Seventh-day Adventists, 1889 Year Book, p. 147, Principle I
text: I. That there is one God, a personal, spiritual being, the creator of all things, omnipotent, omniscient, and eternal; infinite in wisdom, holiness, justice, goodness, truth, and mercy; unchangeable, and everywhere present by his representative, the Holy Spirit. Psalm 139:7.
note: Principle I as printed in 1889: God is “a personal, spiritual being” and “everywhere present by his representative, the Holy Spirit”; the words Trinity, Godhead and “three persons” occur nowhere in the 1872 or 1889 statement.

author: Unsigned statement (corpus lists General Conference of SDA)
work: Fundamental Principles of Seventh-day Adventists, 1889 Year Book, p. 147, Principle II
text: II. That there is one Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of the Eternal Father, the one by whom he created all things, and by whom they do consist; that he took on him the nature of the seed of Abraham for the redemption of our fallen race; that he dwelt among men, full of grace and truth, lived our example, died our sacrifice, was raised for our justification, ascended on high to be our only mediator in the sanctuary in heaven …
note: Principle II (christological clauses) as printed in 1889: “the Son of the Eternal Father, the one by whom he created all things” — no word stands before “Son” (the “[Literal] Son” of a web transcription is an insertion); the rest of II treats the atonement (it cites Acts 3:19; Leviticus 16; Hebrews 8:4, 5; 9:6, 7).

author: Unsigned statement (corpus lists General Conference of SDA)
work: A Declaration of the Fundamental Principles Taught and Practiced by the Seventh-day Adventists (Battle Creek: SDA Publishing Association, 1872), proposition II
text: That there is one Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of the Eternal Father, the one by whom God created all things, and by whom they do consist; …
note: The 1872 wording of the same clause reads “by whom God created all things” where 1889 has “by whom he created”; the Son clause is otherwise identical.

author: Ellen G. White
work: To the Little Remnant Scattered Abroad (broadside, April 6, 1846), describing a vision of February 1845
text: I saw a throne and on it sat the Father and the Son. … The Father’s person I could not behold, for a cloud of glorious light covered him. I asked Jesus if his Father had a form like himself. He said he had, but I could not behold it, for said he if you should once behold the glory of his person you would cease to exist.
note: EGW’s earliest printed account: the Father and the Son on one throne; the Father has a form “like himself” but is covered by “a cloud of glorious light” and cannot be beheld.

author: James White
text: Jesus prayed that his disciples might be one as he was one with his Father. This prayer did not contemplate one disciple with twelve heads, but twelve disciples, made one in object and effort in the cause of their master. Neither are the Father and the Son parts of the “three-one God.” They are two distinct beings, yet one in the design and accomplishment of redemption.
note: James White, 1868: the Father and the Son are “two distinct beings, yet one in the design and accomplishment of redemption”; he denies that they are parts of the “three-one God.”

author: Ellen G. White
text: The Sovereign of the universe was not alone in His work of beneficence. He had an associate—a co-worker who could appreciate His purposes, and could share His joy in giving happiness to created beings. … Christ, the Word, the only begotten of God, was one with the eternal Father—one in nature, in character, in purpose—the only being that could enter into all the counsels and purposes of God. … His “goings forth have been from of old, from everlasting.” Micah 5:2.
note: EGW, 1890: Christ, “the only begotten of God,” was “one with the eternal Father—one in nature, in character, in purpose”; she reads Micah 5:2 as “from everlasting.”

author: E. J. Waggoner
work: Christ and His Righteousness (Bible Students’ Library; announced as “just issued” in GCDB March 19, 1891, page 165.1)
text: The Scriptures declare that Christ is “the only begotten son of God.” He is begotten, not created. As to when He was begotten, it is not for us to inquire, nor could our minds grasp it if we were told. … There was a time when Christ proceeded forth and came from God, from the bosom of the Father (John 8:42; 1:18), but that time was so far back in the days of eternity that to finite comprehension it is practically without beginning.
note: E. J. Waggoner (in print by March 1891): Christ is “begotten, not created,” and “There was a time when Christ proceeded forth and came from God,” so far back that it is “practically without beginning.”

author: Uriah Smith
text: God alone is without beginning. At the earliest epoch when a beginning could be, - a period so remote that to finite minds it is essentially eternity, - appeared the Word. … His beginning was not like that of any other being in the universe. … Thus it appears that by some divine impulse or process, not creation, known only to Omniscience, and possible only to Omnipotence, the Son of God appeared.
note: Uriah Smith, 1898: “God alone is without beginning”; the Son “appeared” “by some divine impulse or process, not creation,” with a beginning “not like that of any other being.”

author: Ellen G. White
text: Still seeking to give a true direction to her faith, Jesus declared, “I am the resurrection, and the life.” In Christ is life, original, unborrowed, underived. “He that hath the Son hath life.” 1 John 5:12. The divinity of Christ is the believer’s assurance of eternal life.
note: EGW, 1898 (the same year as Smith’s Looking Unto Jesus): “In Christ is life, original, unborrowed, underived”; “The divinity of Christ is the believer’s assurance of eternal life.”
